name: Specification
intent: Turn a business rule into a small object that can be tested, named, reused and combined with and, or and not.
scenario: A shop gives a discount to customers who are active, not blocked and have spent at least 100. The same kind of rule is needed on several screens, and it keeps changing.
problem: The rule is an if-chain copied into each screen. When marketing changes it, one copy is edited and the others are forgotten, so two screens disagree. The rule has no name, and a slightly different rule means another copy.
solution: Each condition becomes a Specification with one method, isSatisfiedBy(candidate). Simple ones (Active, Blocked, TotalAtLeast) are leaves. And, Or and Not specifications hold other specifications, so a rule is built by combining them and can describe itself. Every screen asks the same object, and a new rule is a new combination, not a new copy.
pain: The same if-chain is copied into every screen
Changing the rule means finding every copy
The rule has no name and no test of its own
A slightly different rule needs another long condition
benefits: One rule object is used everywhere
A change is made once and every screen follows
Small specifications are tested alone, then combined
A rule can print its own description for logs and error messages
whenToUse: Business rules are reused in several places or change often
Rules are combined in many ways, and some are chosen at run time
You need to explain why a candidate did or did not qualify
whenNotToUse: A condition used once: a plain if is clearer
Rules that never change and are never combined
When the data lives in a database and the rule must run there as a query, unless the specification can also produce one
pitfalls: Filtering millions of rows in memory with isSatisfiedBy instead of in the database
Specifications that reach into other services make a rule slow and hard to test
Too many tiny classes for conditions that are not reused add indirection and no value
Deep and/or/not trees are hard to read: give common combinations a name

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Code that needs to know whether something qualifies, or to select the ones that do.

roles.label: Specification
roles.description: Interface with isSatisfiedBy(candidate) and the combinators and, or and not.

roles.label: Leaf specification
roles.description: One simple condition: active, blocked, total at least N.

roles.label: Composite specification
roles.description: And, Or and Not: they hold other specifications and combine their answers.

quiz.question: The discount rule is an if-chain in six screens. Marketing changes it to require a total of 150, and a month later two screens still use 100. What is the best way to prevent this?
options: Add a comment above each if-chain asking developers to update all six together
Move the rule into a shared helper file and copy the new text from it into each screen
Make one named specification for the rule and have every screen ask that object
Write a test for each screen that checks the number 100 is used in its if-chain
quiz.explanation: The fault is that the rule exists in six places. A single specification object is the one place to change, and all screens ask it. Comments, copying text and per-screen tests all keep six copies that can drift.

quiz.question: A team loads five million customers into memory and calls spec.isSatisfiedBy on each to find the eligible ones. The job is slow and uses a lot of memory. What is the best fix?
options: Give the specification a second form that the repository turns into a query, so the database filters
Run isSatisfiedBy on more threads so that the five million checks finish sooner
Remove the specification and write the condition inside every report that needs it
Cache the result of each customer check in memory so that the next run is quick
quiz.explanation: The slowness comes from moving all rows to the code. A specification that can also describe itself as a query lets the database do the filtering and still keeps the rule in one place. More threads, copies of the condition and a cache keep the full load.

quiz.question: A developer creates IsOver18, IsNotNull and HasName specifications, each in its own class, for conditions used in exactly one place and never combined. What is the likely result?
options: Better tests, because every if statement now has a separate class that can be tested
Faster code, because the classes can be reused by other parts of the system later
A smaller code base, since the classes replace the if statements that existed before
More classes and indirection, without removing any duplication or making rules easier to change
quiz.explanation: A specification pays off when a rule is shared, combined or changes often. For a condition used once it only adds files to read. A plain if is clearer, and it is not shorter in classes or faster.
